item.title: A Factor-Two Lower Bound for Complementing Two-Way Deterministic Finite Automata
item.description: arXiv:2610.18897v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: For every $n\ge22$, we construct a language over a fixed three-letter alphabet whose two-way deterministic state complexity is $n$ and whose complement has state complexity $2n$. Acceptance is at the left endmarker, and infinite computations reject. The lower bound holds for arbitrary deterministic recognizers. The proof uses the group of transformations induced by the witness to constrain the behavior of a smaller recognizer, then derives a contradiction from a permutation query problem. A matching halting complement follows from a $2n$-state construction for sources whose destination states determine the direction of each transition. Splitting states by incoming direction gives a $2n+2b$ upper bound for general sources, where $b$ counts states entered in both directions. In the acceptance-anywhere model of Geffert, Mereghetti, and Pighizzini, the same family has exact complexities $N$ and $2N-1$ for every $N\ge23$.
item.dc:creator: Sudais Arif

item.title: Semi-Linearity and Generalized Stratified Semi-Linearity beyond Context-Free Languages
item.description: arXiv:2610.19562v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Parikh's famous theorem relates to the semi-linearity of context-free languages. We seek for expanding the scope of the semi-linear property from context-free languages to languages beyond them. Of those languages, this work focuses on the languages that are particularly recognized by one-way nondeterministic depth-k storage automata under a natural restriction of frozen blank sensitivity. Those languages (which are called $k$-storable languages) have been already proven to satisfy a natural generalization of the well-known pumping lemmas for regular and context-free languages. The semi-linearity of k-storable languages generalizes Parikh's theorem on the semi-linearity of context-free languages. As for bounded languages, Ginsburg and Spanier's well-known theorem characterizes context-free languages in terms of stratified semi-linearity. This notion is further generalized and is used to characterize the k-storable languages as well. Such a generalization is interesting in its own right. This helps us take an abstract treatment of k-storable languages without relying on "machines". Our results strengthen the belief that those languages are "natural" generalizations of context-free languages.
item.dc:creator: Tomoyuki Yamakami

item.title: Full AFLs Closed under Nested Iterated $k$-Variate Substitution and Depth-k Storage Automata
item.description: arXiv:2610.19584v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Greibach and Ginsburg (1969) studied abstract families of languages or AFLs. A full AFL is a class of languages closed under the following operations: homomorphism, inverse homomorphism, intersection with regular languages, union, concatenation, and Kleene star. Greibach (1970) used a restricted substitution, called nested iterated substitution, to introduce the notion of super AFLs, which are full AFLs that are further closed under nested iterated substitution. The smallest super AFL was shown to be the class of all context-free languages. From this fact, we focus on Greibach's limited, univariable application of nested iterated substitution and further generalize it into k-variate. This introduces the notion of nested iterated $k$-variate substitution whose definition does not rely on "machines". Recently, a "two-tape" version of Hibbard's (1967) rewriting systems, which were later reformulated by Pighizzini and Pisoni (2014) as k-limited automata with "single" input/work tapes, has been studied under the name of depth-k storage automata. This work unearths a few characteristics of the languages recognized by those automata under a restriction known as frozen blank sensitivity in terms of full AFLs and nested iterated k-variate substitution. This will promote a further abstract treatment of those languages.
item.dc:creator: Tomoyuki Yamakami

item.title: Graphs with Bounded Push-Pop Walk Orderings
item.description: arXiv:2610.19724v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Consider a directed graph G and the (generally infinite) set Walks(G) of the walks in that graph. We are interested in ordering Walks(G) as w1, w2,... in a way that ensures that each walk is obtained from the previous one by a bounded number of elementary operations, namely, push operations (which add a new edge at either end of the walk) and pop operations (which remove the first or last edge of the walk). Our goal is to optimize the aforementioned bound, when it exists, in particular when imposing the additional requirement that walks must be ordered in increasing order of length. To this end, we introduce a condition on graphs inspired by earlier work, called inner-connectedness, which is testable in linear time; we show that inner-connected graphs are precisely those which admit bounded walk orderings. Focusing on such graphs, we then introduce and study the pp-rank and the pp-increasing-rank. Namely, the pp-rank of a graph is the best possible bound on the number of push-pop operations in a bounded walk ordering for that graph; and the pp-increasing-rank is the same where we further impose that shorter walks appear before longer walks in the ordering. We show that the pp-rank of inner-connected graphs is in fact always bounded by 3. The pp-increasing-rank of inner-connected graphs is also always finite, but it can be up to linear in the input graph. More precisely, we show that the pp-increasing-rank is related to a new parameter we introduce, the peripherality of graphs. In particular, for cyclic graphs, peripherality is related to the pp-increasing-rank up to multiplicative and additive constants. We last study how to compute these parameters, and show that while peripherality can be computed in polynomial time, the pp-increasing-rank itself is generally NP-hard to compute.
item.dc:creator: Antoine Amarilli, Claire David, Nadime Francis, Victor Marsault, Mika\"el Monet, Yann Strozecki

item.title: The No Endmarker Theorem for One-Way Probabilistic Pushdown Automata
item.description: arXiv:2111.02688v4 Announce Type: replace Abstract: In various models of one-way pushdown automata, the explicit use of two designated endmarkers on a read-once input tape has proven to be extremely useful for making a conscious, final decision on the acceptance/rejection of each input word immediately after reading the right endmarker. With no endmarkers, by contrast, a machine must constantly stay in either accepting or rejecting states at any moment since it never notices the end of the input word. This situation, however, helps us analyze the behavior of the machine whose tape head makes the consecutive moves on all prefixes of a given extremely long input word. Since those two machine formulations have their own advantages, it is natural to ask whether the endmarkers are truly necessary to correctly recognize languages. In the deterministic and nondeterministic models, it is well-known that the endmarkers are removable without changing the acceptance/rejection criteria of each input word. This paper demonstrates that, for a more general model of one-way probabilistic pushdown automata, the endmarkers are always removable. This is proven by employing probabilistic transformations from an "endmarker" machine to an equivalent "no-endmarker" machine at the cost of double exponential stack-state complexity without compromising its error probability. By setting the machine's error probability appropriately, our proof also provides an alternative proof to both the deterministic and the nondeterministic models as well.
item.dc:creator: Tomoyuki Yamakami

item.title: Simple grammar bisimilarity, with an application to session type equivalence
item.description: arXiv:2407.04063v5 Announce Type: replace Abstract: We provide an algorithm for deciding simple grammar bisimilarity whose complexity is polynomial in the valuation of the grammar (maximum seminorm among production rules). Since the valuation is at most exponential in the size of the grammar, this gives rise to a (single) exponential running time. Previously only a double-exponential algorithm was known. As an application, we provide a conversion from context-free session types to simple grammars whose valuation is linear in the size of the type. In this way, we provide the first polynomial-time algorithm for deciding context-free session type equivalence.
item.dc:creator: Diogo Po\c{c}as, Gil Silva, Vasco T. Vasconcelos
